title: Mapping the reactive cysteine landscape of the NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 protein
summary: NOD-like receptor pyring-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) is a cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that drives assembly of an oligomeric inflammasome complex to stimulate pro-inflammatory cytokine production and pyroptotic cell death. Extensive research has shown that NLRP3 activation is dependent on intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Despite this, the precise targets of ROS in this process remain undefined. In this study, a combination of chemoproteomics, in vitro biochemical assays and molecular dynamics simulations were used to characterize reactive Cys and how they may impact NLRP3 conformation and activity status. Affinity-captured NLRP3 was subjected to reverse-thiol trapping to reveal a pool of reactive Cys residues that were identified in subsequent chemoproteomic analyses. C150, C196, and C884 were consistently detected with both in vitro and in cellulo experiments. Several NLRP3 mutants were generated; C150A and C196A (NACHT domain) as well as C933A and C941A (LRR domain) reduced IL-1b output in a reconstituted inflammasome assay. Molecular simulation of Cys sulfenylation in the LRR suggests structural alterations that reposition the trLRR loop to destabilize the inactive NLRP3 structure. Structural modelling provided insights for how Cys oxidation of the LRR may impact on NLRP3 structure. Collectively, the results establish a mechanistic understanding for how ROS may promote NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

title: Structural conservation of the gabapentinoid binding site in human and Caenorhabditis elegans α2δ subunits: a docking and molecular dynamics perspective
summary: Pain is a global health burden requiring effective therapeutic strategies. Gabapentin (GBP) and pregabalin (PGB), used for neuropathic pain, act primarily through alpha2delta subunits of voltage-gated calcium channels. Caenorhabditis elegans expresses UNC-36, an ortholog of mammalian alpha2delta proteins involved in calcium-channel function and nocifensive behavior. However, whether UNC-36 retains the features essential for gabapentinoid recognition remains unclear. We compared human alpha2delta-1 and UNC-36 using sequence and structural analyses, docking, one 500-ns molecular dynamics trajectory per complex, distance-based contact profiling, principal component and free-energy landscape analyses, and MM/GBSA calculations. The modeled proteins showed C-alpha correspondence within a selected 13-residue pocket core (RMSD 0.53 Angstrom), whereas the complete 14-residue mapping yielded 9.07 Angstrom. All four trajectories showed recurrent ligand-protein proximity contacts with residue-level patterns. Aromatic-residue contacts accounted for a larger fraction of contact records in human trajectories, whereas basic-residue proximity was more frequent in UNC-36 trajectories, including recurrent Arg501 and Arg503 contacts. Human alpha2delta-1/PGB showed the lowest ligand RMSD, while alpha2delta-1/GBP showed greater positional variation. In UNC-36, PGB deviated more from its initial pose than GBP. The first two principal components accounted for more conformational variance in UNC-36 complexes than in human complexes. MM/GBSA estimates, without an explicit conformational-entropy contribution, were more negative for PGB than GBP in human trajectories and for GBP than PGB in UNC-36 trajectories. These simulations suggest that selected pocket-core correspondence coexists with differences in modeled contacts, sampled motions, and estimates. They provide hypotheses for investigating gabapentinoid recognition by UNC-36 and its pharmacological relevance.

title: SoluProtMut: Siamese Deep Learning for Predicting Solubility Effects of Protein Mutations with Experimental Validation
summary: Protein solubility is an attractive engineering target because it is a critical property influencing the scalability of protein production and the success of therapeutic proteins in biomedical applications. However, predicting in silico solubility changes upon mutation is challenging due to data heterogeneity and protein bias. Here, we explore how different sources of solubility data can be used for machine learning and present SoluProtMut, a Siamese deep geometric neural network trained to predict the impact of mutations on protein solubility. Our final model was trained exclusively on deep mutational scanning data derived from recombinant protein expression assays in bacterial and yeast systems. We compare our model with five established solubility prediction methods. On an independent set of 44 proteins, the model achieves the highest informedness among the methods compared, with the largest margin for multipoint mutations (a ternary informedness of 26.5%, 8.8 percentage points above the next-best method). Our findings also reaffirm that the scarcity of solubility data continues to hamper progress in this field. To address this limitation, we experimentally quantified solubility changes for 277 single-point and multipoint mutants of haloalkane dehalogenase. Complemented by recent deep-mutational-scanning data on myoglobin, we employed both datasets for external validation. We identify protein-level generalization, rather than model capacity or training-set size, as the main limiting factor in the domain. Integrating high-throughput assays with deep learning nonetheless offers a route to improving the accuracy and scope of solubility prediction.

title: Nucleobase-Specific Recognition of DNA by Protamine
summary: Protamines--arginine (Arg)-rich, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)--replace histones to compact DNA in the sperm nucleus. While folded domains can bind DNA site-specifically, whether IDPs exhibit DNA-sequence specificity remains open. Here, we used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize protamine-DNA binding. Eight copies of salmon protamine (33 residues with 21 Arg) rapidly wrap around a 35-bp DNA molecule. In addition to salt bridges with DNA phosphates, Arg hydrogen-bonds with multiple nucleobases on both strands or the same strand. At the major groove, protamine prefers GC over AT by a 2.6-to-1 ratio, with guanine's O6 and N7 atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors; the preference is especially strong at G-tracts. This selectivity reverses at the minor groove, where AT overtakes GC by a 2.1-to-1 margin. The net effect is a moderate bias for GC over AT in protamine-base interactions. Additional simulations with 20-bp DNA molecules and free-energy calculations reinforce these observations. For experimental validation, we designed DNA sequences with 0-40% GC content. Protamine-DNA mixtures form aggregates, with an increasing propensity at higher GC content and upon shuffling into G-tracts. This work demonstrates that IDPs can bind DNA in a nucleobase-specific manner, with implications for protamine-mediated transcription silencing and remodeling of paternal chromatin.

title: Lateral Membrane Heterogeneity Shapes Antimicrobial Association and Convergent Mechanical Responses
summary: Bacterial membranes are laterally heterogeneous, creating local physicochemical environments that can shape interactions with membrane-active antimicrobials. However, whether this spatial organization only affects local drug association or propagates into collective membrane responses remains unclear. Here we show that lateral membrane heterogeneity shapes antimicrobial association while distinct molecular responses converge on a common loss of membrane mechanical stability. Combining coarse-grained molecular dynamics, giant unilamellar vesicle fluctuation spectroscopy and microfluidic trapping, we follow octenidine, chlorhexidine and polymyxin B from molecular association to vesicle-scale behaviour. All three compounds preferentially associate with domain-associated membrane environments, but differ in how this preference changes with loading and in their effects on lipid mobility. Despite these differences, all three shift the membrane toward a mechanically softer state, while increasing exposure accelerates loss of vesicle stability under flow. These findings identify lateral membrane heterogeneity as an active determinant of antimicrobial response and provide a physical framework for understanding membrane-targeting activity beyond bulk composition and membrane-averaged charge.

title: Bacterial-Mimetic Membranes Reveal Hopanoid-Associated Domain-Like Lateral Heterogeneity
summary: Bacterial membranes are increasingly recognized as laterally heterogeneous assemblies whose local organization can regulate transport, stress adaptation, and interactions with membrane-active compounds. However, the physical principles by which bacterial lipid composition generates spatially distinct membrane environments remain poorly understood, partly because experimentally tractable models that reproducibly exhibit lateral segregation and permit quantitative characterization are limited. Here, we show that a multicomponent, hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membrane spontaneously self-organizes into laterally distinct physical environments that are consistently resolved in experiments and molecular simulations. Giant unilamellar vesicles prepared from a lipid mixture inspired by lipid classes found in hopanoid-producing bacteria, including Methylorubrum extorquens, exhibit stable micron-scale lateral segregation, which is independently reproduced in compositionally matched coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting membrane environments differ in composition, packing, order, mobility, and mechanical properties. Hopanoid-associated domain-like regions are more condensed, more ordered, and less mobile, whereas PE-rich non-domain regions remain more laterally expanded and exhibit faster lipid diffusion. At the global level, the bacterial-inspired membrane displays greater bending rigidity than a fluid phosphatidylcholine reference, while ATR-FTIR measurements independently support increased lipid-chain ordering and denser membrane packing. Together, these findings establish that hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membranes can spontaneously generate coexisting physical environments whose distinct local properties collectively determine global membrane behavior. The resulting experimental-computational framework provides a quantitative basis for investigating bacterial-like membrane heterogeneity and how local composition, dynamics, and mechanics govern responses to membrane-targeting perturbations.

title: Cross-state representation learning enables prospective discovery of dynamic protein allosteric sites
summary: Allosteric regulation offers multifunctional induction in therapeutic interventions, yet conformational plasticity hinders computational identification of allosteric sites. Machine learning models rely on static holo (ligand-bound) structures, generalizing poorly to apo or substrate-bound states where binding pockets are transient or cryptic. We present AsBench2, a cross-state site-recognition benchmark, and AllositeUltra, a deep learning framework integrating multimodal protein representations (combining structure-aware language models with physical dynamics) and residue-guided candidate supplementation, effectively decoupling site detection from static pocket geometry. AllositeUltra demonstrates superior generalization, achieving Top-3 site recovery rates of 65.2% and 70.6% on apo and substrate-bound structures, respectively, representing relative improvements of 36.4% and approximately 50% over the best-performing baselines. Prospective application to MAGI2 identifies a previously unrecognized interdomain allosteric pocket, validated at atomic resolution through small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography. Proteome-wide application yields a high-confidence atlas of targetable allosteric sites, bridging the gap between structural representation learning and prospective AI-driven drug discovery.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Quizartinib Resistance in FLT3 Mutants
summary: Quizartinib, a type II FLT3 inhibitor approved for FLT3-ITD-positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML), is frequently limited by acquired resistance, which arises in up to 40% of patients with disease progression and is driven largely by the D835Y and F691L kinase-domain mutations. To define the underlying mechanisms, we performed triplicate 200-ns all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of wild-type FLT3, FLT3-D835Y, and FLT3-F691L in complex with Quizartinib, combining conformational analysis, MM-GBSA binding free-energy calculations, and binding-pocket characterization. Both mutations destabilized the inactive DFG-out conformation required for type II inhibitor binding, with mean binding free-energy reductions of 5 kcal/mol for D835Y and 10 kcal/mol for F691L relative to wild-type. D835Y disrupted the activation-loop electrostatic network and reduced Cys694 hydrogen-bond occupancy from 85% to 45%, whereas F691L abolished key van der Waals contacts and opened a 120 cubic Angstrom hydrophobic void at the gatekeeper position. Both mutants sampled a wider range of conformations and lost 14-17% of binding-pocket volume. These predictions were corroborated by CCK-8 viability assays and Western blotting of p-FLT3 (Y591) in Ba/F3 cells, which reproduced the predicted resistance hierarchy (F691L > D835Y > WT) at the cellular level. Together, these results indicate that D835Y and F691L confer resistance through distinct electrostatic and hydrophobic mechanisms that converge on destabilization of the inactive kinase conformation, providing a structural basis for the design of next-generation FLT3 inhibitors.
